column1: Logic: XOR vs inclusive OR — what's the difference?
column2:
OR  (inclusive, v) = AT LEAST one true — BOTH is allowed.  T v T = T
XOR (exclusive, +) = EXACTLY one true — both or neither is FALSE.  T + T = F
Mnemonic: XOR = "one or the other, BUT NOT BOTH".
Tell in code: `if (!a && !b) error` rejects only NEITHER -> that's inclusive OR
("at least one"), NOT XOR. XOR must also reject BOTH.

column1: JS: express 'exactly one of a, b' (XOR) in one expression?
column2:
!!a !== !!b
Coerce both to booleans, then "they differ" == exactly one is truthy.
  T,T -> false   T,F -> true   F,T -> true   F,F -> false
(Works for TWO operands only — see the N-operand card.)

column1: JS: the boolean-combination cheat sheet for two flags a, b?
column2:
at least one (OR) : !!a || !!b
exactly one  (XOR): !!a !== !!b
at most one       : !(a && b)          // neither is OK, both is not
both        (AND) : !!a && !!b
neither     (NOR) : !a && !b
not both    (NAND): !(a && b)          // same as "at most one"
=> "optional but mutually exclusive" = at most one = !(a && b)

column1: JS: why doesn't `!!a !== !!b !== !!c` mean 'exactly one of three'?
column2:
Chained !== is PARITY, not "exactly one": it's true when an ODD number are true.
  a=T,b=T,c=T -> true  (three truthy WRONGLY passes)
For N operands, COUNT instead:
  const n = [a,b,c].filter(Boolean).length;
  n === 1  exactly one (real N-ary XOR)   n >= 1  at least one
  n <= 1   at most one                    n === 0 none
Two-operand !!a !== !!b works only because parity and "exactly one" coincide at N=2.

column1: Zod: cross-field rule like 'exactly one of sender / companySender'?
column2:
.refine() on the OBJECT schema — it sees the whole parsed object, returns a boolean.
  z.object({ sender: A.optional(), companySender: B.optional() })
    .refine(d => !!d.sender !== !!d.companySender,
            { error: "...", path: ["sender"] })   // path attaches the issue to a field
Chain more .refine()s for more rules. .superRefine((d, ctx) => ctx.addIssue({...}))
when you need several/targeted issues from one check.

column1: Zod: make a field guaranteed in the OUTPUT without requiring the client to send it?
column2:
.default() — it splits the input type from the output type.
  timestamp: z.iso.datetime().default(() => new Date().toISOString())
INPUT: optional (client may omit).  OUTPUT: required — z.infer types it `string`,
not `string | undefined`, because zod fills it during parse.
(Contrast: dropping .optional() forces the CLIENT to send it -> breaks the contract.)

column1: Boundary rule: which payload shape do you model in a schema?
column2:
The one the PRODUCER actually sends — verified by reading the client, not inferred
from the old server code. (Real case: server validated `sender` with inner company
fields; the frontend actually sent `{sender} | {companySender}` — different keys,
different shapes. The schema would have modelled a fiction.)
